doc_summary: Buck argues that more people should do behavioral ('psychology-style') investigation of language models, building intuition about quirks and failure modes, as a route to skills useful for alignment such as prompt engineering, scary demos, and red-teaming for adversarial training. He frames it as complementary to interpretability and offers to fund and support tooling for such people.

items.claim: prefers deep, hands-on familiarity with a model's behavior over purely internals-based or abstract analysis because good ideas for what to test and what behaviors to explain come from long interaction.
items.quote: Spend a lot of time with them. Write a bunch of text with their aid. Try to learn what kinds of quirks they have; what kinds of things they know and don’t know.

items.claim: Chooses what to test by setting up situations where models are tempted to do bad things, i.e. baby versions of the scary power-seeking/deceptive behaviors, which requires knowing the AI well and prompt engineering.
items.quote: I’m excited for people working on “scary demos”, where we try to set up situations where our models exhibit tendencies which are the baby versions of the scary power-seeking/deceptive behaviors that we’re worried will lead to AI catastrophe.

items.claim: prefers humans who know the AI well hand-crafting tempting inputs for adversarial training over relying on any single method, because it is one useful technique in a smorgasbord but not a full solution against deception.
items.quote: “have humans try to get to know the AIs really well by observing their behaviors, so that they’re able to come up with inputs where the AIs will be tempted to do bad things, so that we can do adversarial training” is probably worth including in the smorgasbord of techniques

items.claim: Probes whether a model relies on proxies versus broader understanding by perturbing natural text and observing how predictions change.
items.quote: Try to figure out where they’re using proxies to make predictions and where they seem to be making sense of text more broadly, by taking some text and seeing how changing it changes their predictions.

items.claim: Hunts for adversarial examples where relatively natural-looking inputs cause weird behavior, i.e. realistic-seeming inputs rather than obviously contrived ones.
items.quote: Try to find adversarial examples where they see some relatively natural-seeming text and then do something really weird.

items.claim: Runs specific experiments across multiple model sizes to see how a behavior or knowledge varies with scale rather than trusting a single model.
items.quote: For many of these experiments, it seems worth running them on LMs of a bunch of different sizes.

items.claim: prefers complementing automated red-teaming tooling with manual human exploration because manual work runs in parallel and gives tool builders concrete users with concrete needs.
items.quote: it seems pretty reasonable for some people to try to just do this work manually in parallel with us automating parts of it. And we’d find it easier to build tools if we had particular users in mind

items.claim: Hedges about the sufficiency of behavioral approaches: useful and worth including, but not something to rely on to solve the whole deception problem.
items.quote: though I definitely wouldn’t want to rely on it to solve the whole problem

items.claim: Wants better tooling than the bare playground for black-box investigation, since fiddly prompt-engineering work benefits from simple code tools.
items.quote: My guess is that this work would go slightly better if you had access to someone who was willing to write you some simple code tools for interacting with models, rather than just using the OpenAI playground.
